articles.title: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
articles.content: Nvidia on Monday announced Jensen Huang has been reinstated as CEO , effective immediately, a dramatic twist in a scandal that hammered the chipmaker's stock price and rocked the tech and artificial intelligence industries. The board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him. The board added that it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and that it is confident Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk." President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had been speaking to Nvidia's board "directly and indirectly," and that Huang "did nothing wrong." Trump said he talked to Huang on Sunday and asked him to promise to "work hard." Huang resigned from his role as chief executive earlier this month after a series of shocking reports about multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The New York Times reported on Sunday that the woman, Alice Huang, was in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security during at least part of the time that she was engaging in a relationship with Huang. Shares of Nvidia closed up 31% following Huang's reinstatement. The stock had shed nearly 33% from the time Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on Nov. 8. The stock closed at $186.64 on Nov.6. "I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process." Stock Chart Icon Stock chart icon Nvidia stock chart. Senior government officials briefed Nvidia's board late last week and communicated that no national security laws were violated, according to sources familiar with the discussion who asked to remain anonymous because they were not authorized to speak publicly. That update prompted the board to reach out to Huang, the people said. Huang and the board held their first conversations since his ouster on Saturday, and the group determined he would return as CEO during a second meeting on Sunday, the people said. Nvidia's cratering stock price played a role in accelerating those conversations. Trump celebrated Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday, writing in a post on his social media site that the board made "the correct and proper decision" to reinstate him. Trump said the U.S. needs Huang's leadership to "ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy." He reiterated that the U.S. government has "no reason to believe" Huang's return poses a risk to national security, and that it "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct." "On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure," Trump wrote. Several tech industry

articles.title: Ladybird is now in alpha
articles.content: Hello friends! Ladybird is now in alpha. You can download it for macOS and Linux. I’ve been looking forward to writing this post for a long time. :^) Ladybird is a browser with a new engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork. The browser around it is modest, but functional. This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details. We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird! The alpha is a rolling channel, and we’ll be pushing out automatic updates regularly. This is the part I’m most excited about. Ladybird improves quickly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that. If you build websites, try yours in Ladybird and tell us what breaks. It supports WebDriver for automated testing, as well as the Firefox DevTools protocol. Thank you to our sponsors and donors, and to everyone who has tested, reported bugs, and written code over the years. There’s still a mountain of work ahead of us, but I’m very happy that you can finally try Ladybird for yourself!
articles.summary: Ladybird 浏览器进入 alpha 阶段，采用自研全新引擎而非分支，现已支持 macOS 和 Linux。

articles.title: New York Bans Subscription and Post-Purchase Fees on Cars
articles.content: Governor Kathy Hochul today signed a bill restricting motor vehicle manufacturers and dealers from charging consumers subscription fees after they purchase a vehicle. Amid rising consumer prices, the new law guards against a rising trend of car companies charging car owners fees to activate and use built-in features like heated seats, enhanced navigation, hands-free driving and entertainment options that do not present an ongoing expense for dealers and manufacturers. “New Yorkers are already struggling with rising prices due to Trump’s affordability crisis, and we’re not going to let harmful business practices increase the cost of living even more,” Governor Hochul said. “People spending their hard-earned money on a car shouldn’t have to fork over even more money for features that should automatically come with the car. My message to car companies is clear: this kind of deceptive business model isn’t going to fly in New York State. Keep your hands out of New Yorkers’ wallets.” S.9348A/A.10411A prohibits motor vehicle manufacturers, dealers or third-party service providers from adding subscription services or charging post-purchase fees for any motor vehicle feature that uses pre-installed components or hardware that do not have an ongoing cost. As vehicles become more advanced, the new law aims to establish clear rules preventing exploitative practices and prevent post-purchase fees as a future automotive business model. New York Attorney General Letitia James said, “No one should have to pay recurring fees just to use features in a car they already bought. My office has secured millions of dollars for New Yorkers throughout the state who were charged illegal junk fees when purchasing a car. Unfair fees are fueling rising costs, and I am proud to work with Governor Hochul and the legislature to bring costs down.” State Senator James Skoufis said, “People ought to know they’re able to use their already-installed remote start or heated seats during the winter without a monthly subscription. This new law will simply and clearly prohibit car manufacturers from ripping off New Yorkers who already paid for vehicle features when they purchased their car. It’s a common sense law and I’m grateful for the Governor and Assemblymember Magnarelli for their partnership enacting this legislation." Assemblymember William B. Magnarelli said, "I thank Governor Hochul for recognizing the importance of this legislation, particularly as technology continues to evolve at a rapid pace. This law will help protect New Yorkers from unfair fees and ensure consumers aren’t paying extra for features already built into their vehicles.” The law will take effect in 90 days on February 27, 2027. This new law is the latest in Governor Hochul’s ongoing commitment to help address the cost of living by putting money back in the pockets of New Yorkers statewide. articles.title: Stalwart is now a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange
articles.content: Nov 23, 2026 - 13 min read For more than twenty years, “the mail server” in most companies meant Microsoft Exchange, and “the mail client” meant Outlook. Today we are releasing Stalwart 1.2.0, and with it Stalwart becomes a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange . Stalwart now implements the protocols that Exchange clients speak: MAPI over HTTP, Exchange Web Services (EWS), Exchange ActiveSync and Autodiscover. Outlook, Apple Mail and the mail apps on phones and tablets connect to Stalwart as they would to an Exchange server, with mail, calendars, contacts, tasks and notes in one account. Users type their email address and password, Autodiscover does the rest, and they keep working in the client they already know. Exchange support is part of the open source Community edition, under the AGPL. Before going into what Stalwart now does, it is worth looking at where self-hosted Exchange stands today, because it explains why so many organisations are looking for a way out. Microsoft has not announced the end of Exchange Server. On paper, on-premises Exchange still exists. In practice, every road Microsoft is building leads to Exchange Online: Exchange 2016 and 2019 are out of support. Both reached end of support on 14 October 2025. Microsoft sold a paid Extended Security Update programme for a while, and according to press reports of an Exchange team statement, it ended in October 2026 with no further extension. Servers still running those versions receive no fixes of any kind. No new features. Exchange Server Subscription Edition (SE) is now the only supported on-premises Exchange, and there will be no more major versions after it. SE does not receive the features developed for the cloud. Even its first cumulative update has slipped from late 2025 to an undetermined date in 2026. The new Outlook does not support it. Microsoft’s own documentation for the new Outlook for Windows says it plainly: “On-premises Exchange accounts aren’t supported.” The APIs are moving to the cloud. New functionality ships only on Microsoft Graph, a cloud API. Exchange Web Services in Exchange Online started being switched off in October 2026 and will be gone entirely in April 2027. None of these steps forces anyone to move on its own. Together, they leave an Exchange administrator with a shrinking set of choices: keep running a server that will not grow, or move the organisation’s mail into Microsoft’s cloud. For many organisations the second option is not acceptable. Email is the record of a company’s contracts, negotiations, legal advice, HR matters and customer data. Placing it with a US provider means placing it within reach of US law, including the CLOUD Act, which allows US authorities to compel American providers to hand over data they control wherever it is stored. Public administrations, healthcare providers, law firms, defence contractors and many European companies cannot accept that, or no longer want to. Data sovereignty means that you decide where your dat

articles.title: Signal is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy
articles.content: Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it. This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data. We’ve already had to do this once with Windows. Last year, we used screenshot blocking to prevent Microsoft’s Recall AI from taking and storing screenshots of your Signal messages on Windows 11 operating systems by default. We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen. The problem is similar to Microsoft Recall on Windows: Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems. This is a significant move. Google (Android), Apple (iOS/macOS), and Microsoft (Windows) produce the three major consumer operating systems (OS), which comprise the environment that third-party developers – like Signal – build their apps to function and operate within. To put it differently, these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem. Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission. In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding. The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy. For over a decade, this guarantee has been backed by our tried and trusted open source code base and our formally verified encryption protocol. These have been scrutinized by some of the best security experts and hackers across the world, and shown to be robust. Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment. All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation. So, we are blocking such capture by preventing screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android. People who want the ability to take screenshots can disable this protection within the Signal app’s settings. However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees. Our remedy is also incomplete – while we ar

articles.title: GitHub Actions accepts invalid YAML
articles.content: TL;DR: GitHub Actions accepts several invalid YAML productions, making it difficult (read: impossible) to parse some real-world action and workflow definitions with a properly conforming YAML parser. This is related to zizmor#1116 , which has been bugging me for a year and a half. Last April, a user reported that zizmor was rejecting a workflow containing a step that looks like this: - name : Create NPM Remote Repository JSON uses : jsdaniell/create-json@v1.2.3 with : name : " npm-remote-template.json " json : ' { "key": "npm-remote", "rclass": "remote", "packageType": "npm", "url": "https://registry.npmjs.org" } ' Apart from the use of a multi-line flow-style string for the json: key, nothing particularly stands out about this step. Except: it isn't valid YAML! YAML says this about flow-style nodes that are nested inside of a block-style parent collection (read: map or array): Flow nodes must be indented by at least one more space than the parent block collection. Note that flow nodes may begin on a following line. Source : YAML 1.2.2 § 8.2.3 That means the correct syntax is instead: - name : Create NPM Remote Repository JSON uses : jsdaniell/create-json@v1.2.3 with : name : " npm-remote-template.json " json : ' { "key": "npm-remote", "rclass": "remote", "packageType": "npm", "url": "https://registry.npmjs.org" } ' The difference is barely visible: - }' + }' YAML is a big and complicated spec, so it didn't even occur to me that this was invalid. Instead, I opened tree-sitter-yaml#36 to "fix" it. I've now opened tree-sitter-yaml#51 to revert that misbegotten fix. On GitHub's side, I'm not sure if they have a clean path towards spec conformance here. Much of the code behind Actions is proprietary, but it seems likely that the underlying parser on their end is YamlDotNet . Actions appears to use YamlDotNet 5.3.0 , which was released in 2018 . However, even upgrading to the newest version (18.1.0 as of writing) wouldn't fix this particular bug, since it's still present on that version (note the !isSingleQuoted guard). My best guess is that a 2020 patch ( YamlDotNet#467 ) only fixed the double-quoted form because YAML's official test suite only tests rule 8.2.3 with a double-quoted string, despite it applying to both forms.
articles.summary: GitHub Actions 接受多种非法 YAML 写法，导致合规解析器无法解析真实工作流定义。

articles.title: Quality IMAP, Part 2: Mailbox Concurrency
articles.content: In the past year, we have been significantly improving the reliability and correctness of Aerogramme's IMAP implementation. This is the second part in a series discussing why implementing IMAP correctly is not so easy, and presenting our work on making Aerogramme's IMAP code as high-quality as we can. Today we focus on challenges that arise when considering concurrent access to a mailbox. Aerogramme is an experimental email server (& calendar, contacts), designed to be geo-distributed, hosted outside of datacenters, on refurbished hardware, and reliable even in presence of network issues and hardware failures. It is built on top of Garage and shares the same philosophy. Aerogramme is AI-free: we do not wish to use unethical technology and prefer to spend effort on careful craftmanship and community-building. This is the second post in a series in which we argue that implementing an IMAP server is not easy , essentially due to two classes of features that are fundamentally challenging to implement. In the previous post , we talked about the first class of features: fine-grained retrieval and querying of email contents. In this post, we talk about the second class of features that make implementing an IMAP server tricky: concurrent access to user mailboxes . Concurrent and distributed software are famously hard to get right; concurrency bugs are known to be hard to find. In our recent work on refining Aerogramme we have tried to approach the problem from different angles. This is the topic of this post: the different ways in which we have improved the correctness of Aerogramme in concurrent settings . This work was funded by NLNet under the " Aerogramme 1.0 " grant, and could not have been possible without their support. Feel free to join the Aerogramme matrix channel for updates or if you just want to chat! Concurrent mailbox access in IMAP A core feature of IMAP is that multiple email clients can simultaneously access the same mailbox. For example, we may want to access our emails both from our phone and our computer. Concurrent access to a mailbox can also happen when a single client is involved: some clients (including Thunderbird) open multiple concurrent connections to a same mailbox to speed up processing. In any case, clients accessing the same mailbox should be able to coordinate between themselves and avoid stepping on each other's toes. Why must clients be able to coordinate when accessing the same mailbox? Assume that we are an email client that sends two commands to read information from a mailbox. Since another client can modify the mailbox in between the two commands, the information we read may have been invalidated by the other client and is now inconsistent! Clients thus need to be able to detect concurrent changes made by other clients . Similarly, a client that reconnects to the server after being offline needs to fetch the changes that happened while it was disconnected. This is possible thanks to mechanisms defined by the IMAP

articles.title: Illiterate Programming
articles.content: My family comes from a part of the world where writing is held in very high esteem. Our poets are national heroes, our role-models are dissident essayists, and our governments, unlike those in Australia and New Zealand, had the good grace to actually attempt to persecute writers because, if nothing else, they knew that those writers would be read. Even now, it's still a cultural expectation that a middle-class Polish adult is at least a little well-read, and they should be able to identify and have read at least three or four poets. It's probably not a surprise, then, that I grew up surrounded by books and grew into a voracious reader as a child. I've always been good at reading and read a lot and, once I'd read enough, I turned out to be a pretty damned effective writer as well. Reading and writing have, in short, always been a massive part of my life to the extent that I almost did an arts conjoint with my engineering degree and when I was dissuaded from that by my parents (one of the biggest regrets in my life, if I'm to be honest), I still did my absolute best to keep up with the humanities as I did my engineering degree (I spent altogether too much time in the library trying to unpick the Latin of the Vulgate bible). And my literacy, little though you might expect it, did me some considerable favours. Being able to write well and lucidly saved me in a couple of engineering courses where I was struggling with the maths, I suspect, and I was able to contribute to magazines and online publications which kept me socially connected despite being a socially awkward mess. It was a jolt, therefore, when I started my third job and found myself, for the first time, interacting with actual programmers. My first job was for an acoustics consultancy, and I was more than a little lucky with it, truth be told: the place was full of sensitive and intelligent music-lovers, some of whom were literary and the rest of whom were at least interested in something worthwhile. My second job involved working heavily with biologists: again, quite a literate crowd, even if some of them were wilfully obtuse about the humanities in the way scientists often are. My third job, though? Nope. Never have I had the misfortune to spend so much time with wilfully ill-read, obtuse, uncultured philistines. And this isn't just me complaining that they don't read Eliot or what-have-you: they had only the barest familiarity with Shakespeare, the bible or any novel at all. Hell, they thought Brandon Sanderson unbearably intellectual, and Sanderson is pretty pulpy as an author. Writing is often a precarious way to make a living, both directly and indirectly. While our situation is stabilising, it's a slow process, which means that if you derive value for my writing, I fear I must ask, as always, for your support. If you'd like to contribute to helping keep me writing, then, you can do so via Patreon , Liberapay or Stripe . In short: programmers don't read, and this vexes me sorely. The

articles.title: Sneakernet
articles.content: NOTICE : Sneakernet is a work in progress. The documentation makes some promises that are not reflected in the current state of affairs. Links to to-be-written parts of the documentation are indicated in red . Sneakernet is a system for securely sending digital messages to other people without using the Internet. Instead, messages are automatically passed on to other Sneakernet users on your local network – at your hackerspace, an event or conference, your local cafe, etc — and then physically carried to their destination on your “sneakers”, where they will be automatically delivered to any recipients on the same network (or handed over to be carried further on by someone else). Sneakernet encourages slow, thoughtful participation in community and face-to-face meetings with the users who will carry your messages onwards to their destination, and entrust their own messages to you. ⇒ Head to Getting started to set up Sneakernet on your device. Many applications can be built on top of sneakernet’s general-purpose messaging system, provided that they are tolerant of high latency and out-of-order messages. Some examples include: Building your own sneakernet applications is easy, too, in any programming language – see Building applications for more details.

articles.title: What VP != VNP Means (In 3 Minutes)
articles.content: I assume you know about the P vs. NP problem. But what is this wacky thing Anthropic just posted ? You learned how to take a determinant in your linear algebra class: det ( 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 ) = 1 ⋅ ( 5 ⋅ 9 - 6 ⋅ 8 ) - 2 ⋅ ( 4 ⋅ 9 - 6 ⋅ 7 ) + 3 ⋅ ( 4 ⋅ 8 - 5 ⋅ 7 ) = 0 The naive way is fine for 3 × 3 matrices, but notice that you need to perform Θ ( n ! ) arithmetic operations here. Exercise for the reader is to find the exact number of operations (hint: start with a recurrence relation). Luckily, if you paid attention, you will remember there are faster ways to do this for big n × n matrices, like Gaussian elimination. If we stick only to adding and multiplying, we can still find a determinant in polynomial time ( there are better ways, but this is an old, readable method ). A related problem to the determinant is finding the permanent. It’s like a determinant without any subtraction: perm ( 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 ) = 1 ⋅ ( 5 ⋅ 9 + 6 ⋅ 8 ) + 2 ⋅ ( 4 ⋅ 9 + 6 ⋅ 7 ) + 3 ⋅ ( 4 ⋅ 8 + 5 ⋅ 7 ) = 450 Unlike determinants, there is no known way to compute permanents in polynomial time. Since finding the permanent of a matrix of 0s and 1s is NP-hard (and in fact #P-complete ), it would be pretty important if there were a way. What the Anthropic proof that VP ≠ VNP means is that there is no way to do this if we are limited to arithmetic circuits of size polynomial in the input-size, which look like this: This means that for P to equal NP, there must be some trick to computing permanents using AND/OR/NOT on the bits of the input that is better than addition and multiplication. There are many problems where access to Boolean operators is helpful, but it isn’t clear how they would help with the permanent. If you think of a way, go claim your $1 million.
articles.summary: 文章用三分钟解释 VP 与 VNP 的区别，回应 Anthropic 近期发布的相关内容。

articles.title: Held together by spare time: Reviving wiki.alpinelinux.org during PHP2Shell
articles.content: It feels like this month (and last month..) has been nonstop chaos. PHP2Shell threw a nice little grenade into an already busy month, and while that was happening a GitLab RCE took down Alpine's GitLab instance . It was a whole thing, and as frustrating as it was, I'm kind of proud to say that I got to help respond to the event and write the incident announcement. Ikke did all of the real heavy lifting, but it takes a community to keep a distribution together. Everything, and I mean everything, is kept together by volunteers lending their time and talent with no expectation that there will be a reward for the effort. We do it because we care for the work being done. Whether it's a critical service enabling a community of tens of thousands to distribute hundreds of petabytes of data that we call "Alpine", or simply enabling a small piece of software to work for personal desires. All of it happens because someone cares enough to do the work. I love this so much, frankly. It's absolutely flabbergasting what we as a community can do with our spare time. I enjoy giving my time to Alpine Linux, because there's a community, and because we can have an outsized impact on the world by collaborating together. It's not perfect, but it's rewarding. I think I owe my career to it in a sense. I've learned so much by simply raising my hand and being willing to give my time and learn a few new things. But there's a limit to how far you get on donated time, both personally, and as a project. Wiki.alpinelinux.org has been languishing a bit Not in the sense that it wasn't used; it gets tons of traffic and contains a treasure trove of useful information that people depend on and are excited to contribute to. But between keeping the infrastructure afloat, migrating off of Equinix to new sponsored compute, and mitigating the constant wave of problems, from scale to RCE, that plague a small engineering team trying to serve a massive consumer base, well, it's no wonder that once alice was no longer contributing, the infrastructure languished a bit. This wasn't intentional, nor was it bad. There simply wasn't spare time to contribute to it. So in November of last year ikke asked if anyone was interested in lending a bit of spare time to fixing that problem. articles.title: Lua for data representation
articles.content: july 23, 2025 lua for data representation my major advocacy is that lua is a very good general purpose language. this is not an opinion shared by all. lua’s major design goal was extending and embedding into existing programs. I think the simplicity and flexibility in design persued towards the end of that goal extends to make lua a very good language in general. that said, it does its job quite well as an embedding language, and one of its more interesting use cases (and actually, one of its oldest use cases) is as a data or configuration format. lua’s syntax provides many niceties. for instance, lua has an infinite family of multiline strings: the most basic one starts with [[ and ends with ]] . however, any amount of equal signs can be put between the two square brackets: print([======[hello, world]======]) . the only way to close a [===[ is with an accompanying ]===] , not with a ]] or a ]==] , or a ]====] . here is a function that for any string, creates the correct multiline string to represent it: local function stringize(str) local equal_signs = "" for e in str:gmatch("](=*)]") do if #e >= #equal_signs then equal_signs = e .. "=" end end return ("[%s[%s]%s]"):format(equal_signs, str, equal_signs) end of course, you can just use string.format with %q , but multiline strings usually provide nicer looking and more compact results. these strings are very good for representing lua code as strings in other lua code. anyway, download this file . if you want to consume massive amounts of memory and possibly crash your computer, run it in cpython. if you want to see “hello, world” printed 5 million times, run it in lua. lua’s parser is designed to handle massive files with stride, which is fairly unique and quite necessary if lua is to be used for this purpose. design and implementation choices like these come together to suit lua for this purpose. I’ve seen 3 main styles of using lua code to represent data or configuration. I think lua manages to accomodate each of them well, and each have their appropriate use. styles of data representation JSON style (LON?) chunks are much like function bodies. they have return values. so, one thing that one can do is just return a big table from a lua program. return { foo = "bar", list = {1, 2, 3}, rule_of_thirds = true, } if you’re using this style, you can omit the return and then prepend it when you load the lua files. this makes any trailing statements syntactically invalid because the return statement must be the last statement in the block. keep in mind, though, that this does not prevent arbitrary code because function literals can be used instead. return (function() arbitrary_code() end)() trying to strip out function literals to make this technique safer is fraught and defeats the general elegance of this technique. one can fairly readily use JSON instead. INI style what is often missed about lua is that it’s subtly full of metaprogrammability. for instance, lua globals are just stored in a table, an

articles.title: Release: Roto v0.14.0
articles.content: Terts November 23, 2026, 3:48pm 1 Roto version 0.14.0 is now available on crates.io ! This is mostly a bugfix release and most users should be able to upgrade without any problems. The only breaking change is around List::contains and List::index when they are used from Rust. For this release, I’d like to thank sha90w and @algernon in particular for both reporting and fixing many issues! As always you can find the release in the following places: You can find the full list of changes below! Language Added Added the List.clear and List.remove methods. ( #500 ) Bug fixes Report an error instead of crashing when trying to assign to a constant. Thanks, @sha90w ! ( #477 ) The lexer now properly handles multi-byte characters in all places. Thanks, @sha90w ! ( #482 ) Fix parsing of char and String literals at the end of input. This issue did not affect Roto in its current state, but enables future work . Thanks, @sha90w ! ( #488 ) Fix the module name of the pkg.roto file of a dependency, which interfered with the pkg.roto of the main package. ( #485 ) Fix panics in cases where an error needs to display a hint in another file than where the error occurred. Thanks, @sha90w ! ( #505 ) Ensure that labels generated by the conversion to MIR are always unique in a function. This didn’t lead to any known problems, but is generally good practice. ( #507 ) Crate Breaking Changes Fix soundness issue and incorrect behaviour of List::contains and List::index . These functions took their arguments by reference, but implementing the correct behaviour required that they take it by value. ( #501 ) Added Added Blob::get_functions_by_signature to get all the functions in a Blob that match a given signature. Thanks, @algernon ! ( #494 ) Make FunctionRetrievalError and TypeMismatch public. Thanks, @algernon ! ( #503 ) Bug fixes Fix DynVal being used in combination with vtables in the library! macro. Thanks, @sha90w ! ( #488 ) Filter out generated functions from the hints generated by Blob::get_function . Thanks, @algernon ! ( #496 ) Fix extracting tests from a Blob with tests in a dependency. ( #499 ) Fix a panic when displaying symbols that are not in a package, such as registered items. This panic was also triggered when such a symbol was used in the signature of an extracted function. ( #497 ) Documentation The manual has a new look and has been improved in a few places. ( #480 )
articles.summary: Roto v0.14.0 发布到 crates.io，以修复 bug 为主，仅 Rust 侧 List::contains 与 index 有破坏性变更。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #543: Google is the latest tech giant to chase TypeSafe's 8-week-old Jev
articles.content: This issue is about decision models, a new kind of AI model that does not write text. On Wednesday Google released its own, after OpenAI and Microsoft did in October, and all three charge $0.10 or less per million input tokens and nothing for output. Shanghai AI Lab says its 4B model beat Jev on its tests, and Microsoft built its model on Alibaba's Qwen. Chatbots still score a little higher on the hardest decisions, at 15 times the cost. In the middle: on Vercel's gateway, decision models took one in four AI requests in October.

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: 高校IT负责人首次将AI列为首要优先事项，剑桥因AI训练条款拒绝Turnitin新协议，达特茅斯调查教务长写作，Ken Griffin向卡内基梅隆捐赠30亿美元。

articles.title: A seminal moment in computing
articles.content: MG, founder and CEO of WorkOS, is back to talk about leading a company through what DHH called a seminal moment in computing. He explains Atlas, the AI coworker WorkOS built for itself and then launched, why agents will soon choose and sign up for your tech stack, and why this moment feels closer to fire than to the iPhone. Then he gets practical: starting a company is easier than ever, but product-market fit is harder, so be a heat-seeking missile for pain, pick customers you like, and stop calling yourself non-technical.
articles.summary: WorkOS创始人兼CEO MG做客播客，谈带领公司度过DHH所称的计算时代关键时刻，介绍自研AI同事Atlas，并预测代理将自主选择并注册技术栈。

articles.title: Orbin' with Amp
articles.content: Quinn Slack is back and we're talking about the next level for Amp. Agents write the code, they review the code, and they can push it to main (like our friends at Amp). But where should your agents live? Who remembers what you actually asked them to do? Amp is now its own company, and Quinn has a lot to say about orbs, threads that last forever, and why code review as we know it is fading. He explains why the model matters less than it used to, and why he worries we could lose the open source commons. Quinn even built a feature request live on the show to solve my tailnet problem.
articles.summary: Quinn Slack回归播客谈Amp新阶段：代理编写、审查并推送代码至主分支，Amp已成为独立公司，探讨代理应部署何处及如何记住用户指令。

articles.title: All your packages are belong to us
articles.content: AI agents can write the code, choose the packages, and run the install. Who's checking what they just invited onto your machine? This week I'm joined by Ahmad Nassri, CTO of Socket and former CTO of npm. We get into the trust built into a package install, the new ways attackers are using agents, and what it takes to keep building without handing over the keys or your wallet.
articles.summary: Socket CTO 探讨 AI 代理自动选包安装带来的供应链安全风险，以及攻击者利用代理的新手法。

articles.title: We now have Kerr’s Law
articles.content: Dave Kerr created hacker laws, and now he finds himself reviewing agent-written code for them. Back on the show after six years, Dave names what he sees limiting teams today: keeping everyone’s mental model in sync with what’s actually been built. Adam declares it Kerr’s Law on the spot. We get into why Dave’s team treats code review as a deliberate slowdown, how Shellwright lets agents bring evidence to a pull request, and what living with bipolar disorder has taught Dave about noticing when the excitement of these tools stops being healthy.
articles.summary: Dave Kerr 提出团队瓶颈在于心智模型与实现脱节，被命名为 Kerr 定律，并讨论审查代理代码的挑战。

articles.title: The future is Postgres
articles.content: Craig Kerstiens returns to talk about the ever-expanding world of Postgres: a deliberately boring core, a thriving extension ecosystem, and pg_lake bringing DuckDB and Iceberg into the mix. We dig into the pain of ETL, what Craig is watching in Postgres 19, the impact of AI on open source maintainers, and why the database still has plenty of room to grow.
articles.summary: Craig Kerstiens 谈 Postgres 扩展生态、pg_lake 集成 DuckDB 与 Iceberg，以及 AI 对开源维护者的影响。

articles.title: Building what's next
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Zeno Rocha, CEO of Resend, about scaling "boring" email to 3 million users, the secret Go rewrite behind it, and building for agents. We cover pricing.md, MCP, spam gangs, and why Resend keeps what's next for email.
articles.summary: Resend CEO Zeno Rocha 分享用 Go 重写支撑 300 万用户的邮件服务，并布局面向 AI 代理的产品。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: Gavriel Cohen 将周末项目 NanoClaw 打造成爆红开源项目，以容器隔离方案解决 AI 代理安全问题。

articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.

We cover $5 PlanetScale Postgres, the Neki "do-over" of Vitess, agents shipping schema changes through deploy requests, rolling back a 500TB table in seconds, and the very real question of whether to open source any of it. articles.title: Google Is Finally Retiring the Nest App Early Next Year
articles.content: Google is shutting down its 15-year-old Nest app on January 25, 2027, requiring users to switch to Google Home to remotely control their smart home devices and receive notifications. "Then, on August 2, the company will retire Google Assistant on smart speakers and displays, with Gemini replacing the older tech for voice controls," reports Engadget. From the report: If you've yet to migrate your Nest devices to the Google Home app, the company says your existing settings and schedules will transfer over automatically. The only thing you need to manually move over are any custom clips you might have saved over the years. You can do this by visiting the Nest website before January 25 and clicking the "Download all" button. Google says it will automatically migrate Nest Aware (1st Gen) subscriptions to its newer Google Home Premium package. "You will receive an email closer to the date of transfer detailing your subscription information," the company adds. "The Nest app launched over 15 years ago, and home technology has changed a lot since then," Google says of the decision. "To give every Nest user Google's latest security protections and most advanced cyber defenses, plus new features from Gemini, we're bringing all Nest devices together in the Google Home app." Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: Google 将于 2027 年 1 月停用 15 年的 Nest 应用，8 月以 Gemini 取代智能音箱上的 Assistant。

articles.title: Trump Halts Army's Plans to Detonate Bomb-Making Chemicals In Iowa
articles.content: President Trump has ordered the military to halt plans to detonate nearly five tons of unstable lead azide explosives at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. "Trump claimed that the fate of the unstable, highly explosive material is now in the hands of a federal court and Rob Sand, Iowa's governor-elect, who won't be sworn into office until January," reports Ars Technica. From the report: The Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups. The explosion will launch a plume of toxic gases and neurotoxic lead that could reach up to 100 miles away from the Iowa facility, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP). Iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand. The environmental groups, led by Earthjustice, claimed in an emergency court filing that the Army had not fully considered safer options for disposing of the lead azide before planning the detonation. Late Thursday, a federal appeals court granted Earthjustice's request to put a hold on the Army's permit from the Environmental Protection Agency, which allowed for the controlled detonation to be carried out. Around the same time, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the detonation would be postponed until Monday so the military could communicate with Iowans about the situation and plans. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 特朗普叫停陆军在爱荷华州引爆近五吨不稳定叠氮化铅炸药的计划，称交由联邦法院处理。

articles.title: Jensen Huang Says He'll Be a 'Better CEO' As Staff Applauds His Return
articles.content: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang received a standing ovation from employees upon returning to the company's headquarters Monday, less than two weeks after resigning amid revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving an alleged Chinese spy. "Thank you all for the second chances. I'm gonna be a better CEO the second time around," Huang told staff. His reinstatement followed intervention by President Trump and Vice President JD Vance, with Nvidia's board saying it received assurances from senior U.S. officials that Huang's return posed no national security risk. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: CrowdStrike to Buy Zscaler In $44 Billion Deal
articles.content: CrowdStrike has agreed to acquire network security provider Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal. "The deal marks CrowdStrike's biggest acquisition to date and is among the largest in the sector as businesses consolidate and ramp up defenses to fend off AI-powered attacks," reports CNBC. The acquisition is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028. From the report: "With Zscaler, we're building cybersecurity's operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely," CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said in a statement. "We see a path to become the largest AI safety and security company the world has ever seen." CrowdStrike has been a major beneficiary of skyrocketing demand for AI security, with shares soaring about 80% this year as of Monday's open. Zscaler shares are up about 5% year to date after Monday's surge. Their combined market value exceeded $265 billion as of Friday's close, behind market leader Palo Alto Networks at $282 billion. [...] Analysts view the Zscaler deal as a major AI security opportunity, allowing CrowdStrike to capture more customer security spending and close a significant gap with Palo Alto. "The addition of ZS to CRWD's platform could bring more breadth in an era of vendor consolidation and, more importantly, network security to position the company more effectively for rising demand for AI Sovereignty," wrote analysts at JPMorgan. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: CrowdStrike 以 439 亿美元全股票交易收购 Zscaler，为其最大并购，旨在应对 AI 驱动的攻击。

articles.title: Trump Is Said to Have Directed Effort to Reinstate Nvidia Chief
articles.content: President Trump reportedly directed a behind-the-scenes effort to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO, enlisting Vice President JD Vance to secure assurances from federal officials that Huang was not facing criminal charges or considered a national security risk. According to The New York Times, the intervention came despite intelligence concerns surrounding Huang's alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese spy linked to an investigation into illegal Nvidia chip shipments to China. From the report: [...] Only a tiny handful of officials at the highest level of the government were aware of these conversations. On Sunday night, Nvidia's board told the administration that it would be announcing Mr. Huang's reinstatement on Monday morning before the markets opened. The announcement included a note about a new compliance committee, intended to offer public assurance that the company was taking seriously the investigation into the possible smuggling of advanced chips. Mr. Trump was said to have been thrilled that the plan to restore Mr. Huang was executed without any leaks. In directing Mr. Vance to engage with Mr. Huang and his peers, Mr. Trump was turning to one of the members of his administration with the strongest relationships in Silicon Valley. The vice president is close to some of Mr. Huang's biggest supporters and admirers, such as David Sacks, the investor and co-chairman of the President's Council of Advisers on Science and Technology. Mr. Sacks previously served as Mr. Trump's key adviser on artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency issues. On Monday morning, Mr. Trump rejoiced in Nvidia's action, saying on his social media website Truth Social that the company "made the correct and proper decision." The president explicitly connected the reinstatement of Mr. Huang to the health of the U.S. economy. "The Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy," Mr. Tru

articles.title: YC Startup Working On 'Cost Per Kill' For Missiles
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: At 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he's not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided-missile startup. In September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator's fall 2026 cohort. The startup accelerator counts companies like Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash, and Reddit among its alumni; Dandzbergs is likely the youngest solo founder in its vaunted history. His startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a new class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts. "I think missiles are the coolest thing," Dandzbergs tells WIRED. "A lot of people that have found success in engineering early on have had a passion for blowing stuff up." In conversation, Dandzbergs is poised and articulate. He talks about "attacking hard problems," breaking things down to "first principles," and how the Ukraine conflict has forever altered the theater of war -- a personal fixation, given his country's proximity to Russia. He projects an unassailable confidence in his own abilities. "He's a pretty exceptional person," says Harj Taggar, a YC partner assigned to mentor Dandzbergs. "I'm still somewhat in disbelief that we're talking about a 16-year-old." Dandzbergs has resolved to apply these unusual talents to figuring out how to optimize targeted killing. His startup's guiding ambition, according to its investor one-pager, is to bring down the "cost per kill." Dandzbergs hopes to demonstrate a prototype missile by December. Despite concerns about the ethical implications of autonomous weapons and his young age, he remains undeterred. "I want to be part of it. I want to move with the future of warfare," he says. "Please don't say I'm sacrificing my childhood," says Dandzbergs. "This is the childhood I dreamed of." Read more of this story at
articles.summary: 16 岁少年创办 YC 支持的 AI 制导导弹初创公司，主打“单次击杀成本”概念并获 50 万美元。

articles.title: US Intelligence Chief Predicts More Tech Outages As Systems Undergo Upgrades
articles.content: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Sunday that Americans should expect more technology outages as companies and government agencies modernize aging infrastructure. Speaking on CNN, Clayton said the upgrades are necessary to improve performance and cybersecurity but will inevitably cause "glitches, gaps, [and] interruptions in service." Reuters reports: A string of technology failures this month disrupted critical U.S. systems, including a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage that hit email services, a technical glitch that affected several major banks, and a temporary disruption to the National Security Agency's network. Speaking on the ABC program "This Week," Clayton reiterated his previous statements that those outages were not the result of coordinated or state-sponsored actions, attributing them to technical upgrades. Clayton declined to discuss specifics of separate reports of cyberattacks on the FBI and Department of Agriculture, saying he expects investigators to provide answers "in due course." Clayton told CNN: "The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road." Microsoft President Brad Smith issued a similar warning on CBS News' Face the Nation: "I think we have to be prepared, frankly, for the coming months because this isn't the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks ... The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now." Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 美国情报总监警告，随着企业和政府升级老旧基础设施，民众应预期更多技术中断。

Discover dealerships, search real inventory, verify vehicle facts and prices with rebates, and send customer-approved inquiries. Dealers can also offer trade-in valuation and credit applications. A buyer client needs only its chosen binding. AAP does not require a dealer-side language model or a new CRM. A working MCP endpoint is required. articles.title: JavaScript Geometry Orthogonalize library
articles.content: JavaScript Geometry Orthogonalize library Squares the corners of GeoJSON lines and polygons (e.g. building footprints), so that every segment becomes horizontal or vertical on an orthogonal grid, aligned either to the cardinal directions or to the dominant orientation of the shape. Orthogonalize(options, geojson) accepts any GeoJSON object (Geometry, Feature or FeatureCollection) containing LineString/Polygon geometries and returns a new orthogonalized GeoJSON; the input is not modified. articles.title: Sometimes three boring statements beats one clever expression
articles.content: Modern JavaScript gives us a lot of expressive tools. Sometimes a little too many. Optional chaining, nullish coalescing, ternaries, spread, template literals. I like all of them and use them every day. But together, they make it really easy to cram a lot of logic into a single expression. I used to think that was a sign of good JavaScript. I’m not so sure anymore. When one more ?? is too many Take something like this: const theme = config?.theme ?? user?.preferences?.theme ?? defaults.theme; I’ve written this plenty of times. It’s short and it works. But once these expressions start growing, they read more like puzzles than code: const theme = config?.theme ?? user?.preferences?.theme ?? getFallbackTheme() ?? defaults.theme; I can follow it, but I have to stop and parse it. Compare that to this: let theme = config?.theme; if (theme == null) { theme = user?.preferences?.theme; } if (theme == null) { theme = getFallbackTheme(); } return theme ?? defaults.theme; More lines? Sure. But it’s a lot more obvious. Yes, I give up const and reassign a variable. I’ll take that trade. Long expressions hide decisions Longer expressions squeeze several decisions into one piece of syntax. The more you chain, the more you have to work out at once: What happens if config is undefined? Where does the fallback come from? Which value wins? What if getFallbackTheme() throws? Chaining saves some vertical space, but you have to hold more in your head. It’s a practical problem, too. You can’t put a breakpoint on one fallback in the middle of a ?? chain, and you can’t log a single step without rewriting the expression. With separate statements, every step gets its own line to stop on or log. The diffs are nicer, as well. Adding a fallback means adding a block, not editing one dense line. Plain statements are fine A lot of us started treating plain if statements as something to avoid. So we’d rather write this: return user?.isAdmin ? getDashboard(user) : getLandingPage(user); than this: if (user?.isAdmin) { return getDashboard(user); } return getLandingPage(user); Neither one is objectively better. The second isn’t “less modern,” it’s often just easier to read. A single ternary like that is fine. It’s when they nest that I stop: return isLoading ? "Loading" : error ? "Failed to load" : items.length === 0 ? "Nothing here yet" : `${items.length} items`; The same thing with plain statements: if (isLoading) return "Loading"; if (error) return "Failed to load"; if (items.length === 0) return "Nothing here yet"; return `${items.length} items`; Clever code gets old fast Over the past couple of years I’ve found myself chaining less and writing fewer nested ternaries. I don’t mind adding another if anymore. I care more about readability than being clever. When I’m debugging production code or reviewing a pull request, I can’t remember ever wishing something had been written as one bigger expression. My rule of thumb is simple. A chain of plain values is fine. Once there’s a functi

From a local command to a release pipeline, keep execution, credentials and data under your control. Security and privacy are part of the execution contract. articles.title: Dual JWT Authentication: Security, Redis, and Trade-Offs
articles.content: Authentication is one of those backend features that looks simple until you need to make it secure, scalable, and inexpensive. A user logs in, receives a token, and includes it in subsequent requests. The server verifies the token and allows access. Easy enough. But real applications need more than that. Users expect to stay signed in for weeks, log out from multiple devices, recover from interrupted connections, and have their sessions terminated when credentials are compromised. Meanwhile, backend teams want to avoid unnecessary database queries on every authenticated request. These requirements pull authentication architecture in different directions. One possible compromise is a Dual JWT architecture : short-lived access tokens sent through the Authorization header, longer-lived refresh tokens stored in secure cookies, and a small Redis-backed mechanism for revoking sessions. The approach can reduce database traffic significantly. But its security properties depend on how refresh tokens are managed, how revocation works, and which attacks the application needs to defend against. Let’s examine the architecture, its implementation in Node.js, and the trade-offs that are easy to overlook. 1. Why a Single Token Is Often Not Enough Consider an application that uses one JWT for authentication. After login, the server issues a token: Authorization : Bearer eyJhbGciOi... Every protected API request includes that token. The server verifies its signature and expiration time without querying a session database. This is convenient, but the token’s lifetime creates a problem. If it expires after 15 minutes, users need a way to obtain another token without repeatedly entering their credentials. If it remains valid for 30 days, stealing it may give an attacker access for a long time. Neither option is particularly attractive. What About Cookie-Based Sessions? Traditional session authentication usually stores an opaque session identifier in an HttpOnly cookie. The browser sends that cookie automatically, and the server looks up the associated session. This approach has important advantages. Tokens aren’t exposed to ordinary JavaScript through document.cookie , and individual sessions can be invalidated centrally. However, cookie-based authentication also requires appropriate CSRF defenses because browsers attach eligible cookies automatically. That doesn’t make cookie sessions inherently insecure. Properly implemented server-side sessions remain an excellent choice for many web applications. The question is whether the application needs the additional flexibility of separate access and refresh credentials. 2. Two Tokens, Two Responsibilities The Dual JWT approach separates API access from session renewal. Property Access token Refresh token Purpose Access protected APIs Obtain new access tokens Format JWT JWT in this design Lifetime 5–15 minutes Up to 30 days Transport Authorization header Secure cookie Client storage Memory HttpOnly cookie Verification Loca
articles.summary: 文章探讨双 JWT 认证方案，分析其在安全性、Redis 存储与性能成本之间的权衡，为后端开发者提供可扩展且低成本的认证设计思路。

articles.title: pathmask matches relative paths against patterns in the syntax of .gitignore
articles.content: Match paths using .gitignore syntax. Use pathmask to filter files by including or excluding matching paths. Requires Node.js 20 or newer. ESM only. Create a mask from patterns and test each path with matches() . import { PathMask } from 'pathmask' ; const mask = new PathMask ( [ 'src/**/*.js' , 'docs/' , '*.md' , '!CHANGELOG.md' , ] ) ; mask . matches ( 'src/index.js' ) ; // true mask . matches ( 'src/cli/run.js' ) ; // true mask . matches ( 'test/index.js' ) ; // false mask . matches ( 'docs/logo.png' ) ; // true mask . matches ( 'local/logo.png' ) ; // false mask . matches ( 'README.md' ) ; // true mask . matches ( 'test/README.md' ) ; // true mask . matches ( 'CHANGELOG.md' ) ; // false Tools often get a list of paths from a config and need to filter it, for example to choose which files to build, lint or deploy. The .gitignore syntax is the format every developer already knows for such rules. It is based on the basic POSIX glob syntax with * , ? and [...] , and adds a few simple rules for lists of paths. pathmask tests a given path against these rules and follows the behavior of git, so a pattern means the same here and in .gitignore . Short rules: a pattern without / matches at any depth, dist/ matches a directory with all its contents. Exceptions: patterns are applied in order, ! brings a path back. Dotfiles: * matches names that start with . , no options needed. One reference: git defines the behavior, there are no library-specific options. For common rules, the .gitignore syntax is shorter and easier to read than glob. glob pathmask ['**/node_modules/**', '**/*.log'] ['node_modules/', '*.log'] ['**/*.log', '!**/keep.log'] ['*.log', '!keep.log'] ['**/dist', '**/dist/**'] ['dist/'] ['**/.*'] with the option { dot: true } ['.*'] To write glob patterns with {a,b} and extglob in pathmask, see Glob equivalents . Creates a path matcher from an array of patterns in .gitignore syntax. Parameter Type Description patterns string[] Patterns in .gitignore syntax, see Patterns . Throws a TypeError when patterns is not an array of strings, see Errors . Tests a relative path against the patterns. Parameter Type Description path string A path relative to the root, see Paths . Returns true if the mask matches the path or a directory that contains it. Otherwise, returns false . Throws a TypeError when the path is invalid, see Errors . Keep the paths that the mask does not match. Create the mask once and reuse it for all paths. const excluded = new PathMask ( [ 'node_modules/' , '*.log' , '.*' ] ) ; const paths = [ 'README.md' , 'debug.log' , '.env' , 'src/index.js' , 'node_modules/ansis/index.js' ] ; const files = paths . filter ( ( file ) => ! excluded . matches ( file ) ) ; // ['README.md', 'src/index.js'] Exclude files in a directory Read the files of my-project and keep the files that the mask does not match. import { readdirSync , statSync } from 'node:fs' ; import path from 'node:path' ; import { PathMask } from 'pathmask' ; const rootPath = './my-pro

articles.title: Announcing Parcel 3 Alpha
articles.content: Announcing Parcel 3 alpha 2026-11-04 Today we're releasing the first alpha of Parcel 3, a ground up rewrite of Parcel in Rust. It is up to 100x faster than v2, and supports native plugins written in Rust, Go, Swift, or C, as well as a custom runtime for JavaScript and TypeScript plugins. It also includes improved automatic code splitting, library mode, tree shaking, centralized configuration, and much more. In Parcel v2, we rewrote several individual pieces of Parcel in Rust. First was our JavaScript compiler , built on top of SWC. Then, we built Lightning CSS . Later, we rebuilt our HTML and SVG transformer and optimizers. However, Parcel's core was still written in JavaScript. This limited our maximum possible performance due to lack of shared memory between threads, high memory usage, garbage collection, and the cost of serializing values between workers and languages. Parcel v3 is an entirely self-contained Rust binary, with no dependency on Node at all. Everything from the CLI and dev server, to the transformers, bundler, optimizers, and everything in between is now fully native. This enables us to efficiently take full advantage of modern multi-core hardware. The results speak for themselves: up to 100x faster builds using the same underlying compilers as v2, only changing the core. Let's cut to the benchmarks. Here's a comparison of cold development builds between v2 and v3 for React Spectrum , a large TypeScript monorepo. For reference: Storybook : ~100 entries, JS macros , custom plugins ported to Rust for Parcel 3. Docs website : ~340 pages, React Server Components, MDX, Tailwind, custom plugins. Library build : ~160 packages, TSX, macros, CSS modules, SVG icons. Outputs over 14,000 files. Cold development build time, Parcel 2 vs Parcel 3 Storybook: Parcel 2 16.62s, Parcel 3 572ms (29× faster). Docs website: Parcel 2 87.59s, Parcel 3 810ms (108× faster). Library build: Parcel 2 131.47s, Parcel 3 2.71s (49× faster). articles.title: Goyangi: watch what Claude Code is doing, live: every step, tool call, subagent, token and cost in a side panel
articles.content: Goyangi is a panel beside your Claude Code conversation that shows, turn by turn, where the time and money went. Goyangi (고양이) is the Korean word for a cat: a cat that sits next to the conversation and watches every turn. claude plugin marketplace add netil/goyangi claude plugin install goyangi@goyangi --scope user Run /reload-plugins , then open the panel with /goyangi . It also opens by itself when a session starts. New versions install automatically (turn this off in the settings screen, = in the header). Sessions and browser tabs have numbers, so a short prompt is enough: send this to session 2 pull from 1 Summarize the docs tab Work in tab B3 send this to session 2 passes this session's handoff note to the other session. pull from 1 asks session 1 for its handoff Summarize the docs tab and Work in tab B3 work in that very browser tab, with your sign-ins. The numbers come from the Open sessions and Browser tabs boxes When context passes the alert threshold, click Continue in a fresh session and the work carries on in a new session from a handoff note Turn flow : every model request, tool call, and subagent of the turn in order, with tokens, cost, and a time share bar Gauges and advice : context, cache hit rate, and the 5h and 7d usage limits with a forecast. Rule-based advice flags repeated failures, cache drops, and files read again. All computed locally, no tokens spent Session map and log : one row per turn to compare, and a replay of any recent turn. The log switches between key events and everything Walk and compact views : press v and a pixel cat or dog walks through the turn, its mood showing context, cost, and usage limits. Press again for a compact two-row track of the steps Forks : start a prompt with ; and it runs in a background session in its own git worktree while you keep working here. Its permission requests come to this panel, and it merges back when its tests pass Fresh session : past a token point (200k by default), the work moves to a new session in the same window with a handoff note instead of compacting Prompt hold : in a long session, a prompt typed after the prompt cache expired, or one a small model reads as off topic, is held before it is sent, and Goyangi asks whether to send it here or in a fresh session Open sessions : send this session's handoff to another Claude Code session or a coding agent (Codex, OpenCode, ...), or pull theirs here Browser tabs : your open tabs, numbered. Say "B3" or "the GitHub PR tab" and the model works in that tab Terminal and desktop app : the same panel in both The walk view's cat and dog: running, thinking, working, failing, and sleeping. See the manual for the layout, shortcuts, advice rules, and settings . Claude Code with mod (function hooks) support The walk view's pixel art uses octant characters (Unicode 16) in Ghostty, kitty, and WezTerm. articles.title: We Migrated 10,144 Tests from Jest to Vitest in 3 Weeks: The Honest, AI-Assisted Truth
articles.content: A note on the Vitest version: This migration was carried out in August 2026, using Vitest 4 . All the figures, benchmarks, configuration details, and lessons described in this article refer to Vitest 4, not Vitest 5. Migrating a test runner is rarely a magic "swap and go" operation. Our experience moving our entire frontend test suite from Jest to Vitest was a real engineering undertaking, filled with bottlenecks, meticulous pool tuning, unmasked bugs, one rollback, and one optimization we shipped and then had to take back. Over the course of about three weeks, our frontend team migrated eight repositories. We didn't settle for file counts; we ran every suite end-to-end to get the real numbers. Here is the exact scale of what we achieved: 10,144 executed unit tests, real numbers from actually running the suites, not file counts. 1,799 test files across 8 repositories. 0 repos left in a half-migrated state. ~3 weeks to complete the entire effort, migrations plus the tuning that followed. ~$751 estimated AI token cost for the Claude Code sessions we could trace to this work. See the caveats on that number below: it's a rough upper bound, not a bill. This is the story of what actually happened, drawn directly from our git history, PR bodies, and session logs, to help you navigate your own migration. To save you some of the pain we went through, we also published a generalized version of the AI automation skill we ended up wishing we'd had from day one: github.com/Subito-it/articles-code/tree/main/jest-to-vitest-migration . Why Jest started hurting We didn't decide to migrate just because "Jest is slow" in the abstract. We migrated because maintaining it had become an active, recurring tax on our engineering time. We also wanted to be on the side of where the ecosystem was heading, since Vitest was fast becoming the default choice for new Vite/Next.js projects. 1. The CommonJS vs. ESM nightmare By default, next/jest skips transforming anything inside node_modules , so when a dependency ships an ESM-only update, Jest's CommonJS require() fails. We found ourselves hand-patching transformIgnorePatterns regexes to allow-list specific packages. Here's the exact code comment from our config, verbatim: // ESM-only node_modules that Jest must transform. next/jest overwrites any // user-supplied transformIgnorePatterns to skip all of node_modules, so we // allow-list these on the resolved config instead. const esmPackagesToTransform = [ ' cookie ' ]; Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Separately, and about six weeks before we'd even decided to migrate: a major version bump of uuid shipped as pure ESM and broke Jest outright. The real commit message: "uuid v14 ships as pure ESM which breaks Jest (CommonJS). Replace the single usage of uuid() ... with the native crypto.randomUUID() ... removing the dependency entirely." Rather than fight the transform config again, the team just deleted the dependency. When your test runner is dictating your dependency

articles.title: 2026 年我的常用 Mac 软件分享
articles.content:
![2026 我的 Mac 常用软件，按自己做的、产品开发、上网、效率四组排列的 24 个软件图标](https://cdn.tw93.fun/blog/pic/mac-apps-2026.webp)

每年固定节目，给大伙分享我这一年每天都在用的不错 Mac 软件，由于有了 AI 以后反而常用软件少了很多，只有这 24 个了，看看哪些是大伙也经常在用的，也欢迎推荐你认为 2026 你最喜欢的软件给我。

打算想到啥说啥，先看到哪一个说哪个，不按照上图顺序来给大伙分享。

1. [**Mole**](https://mole.fit/)：几乎每天会用来清理一遍垃圾以及看菜单栏看系统的状态，包括里面的卸载、不息屏、风扇小工具每天会使用，同时每天都会来迭代它。
2. [**Claude Code**](https://www.claude.com/product/claude-code)：我现在主要用 CLI，几乎每时每刻都在跑，默认 Opus 5.5 high，复杂就 Fable 5.2 medium，现在没有用 Codex 了，也没有用啥多 Agent 工具，我喜欢简单可控的编码。
3. [**Kaku**](https://kaku.fun/)：我喜欢简单默认好看轻量的终端工具，每天在上面多 Tab 跑 Claude，我喜欢用黑色背景的 TUI 搭配 [JetBrains Mono](https://www.jetbrains.com/lp/mono/) 代码字体，这个字体依然是我最近三年最喜欢的代码字体。
4. [**ego lite**](https://lite.ego.app/)：今年最让我惊喜的一个浏览器，简单漂亮好用，之前我主要是用 [Helium Browser](https://helium.computer/)，假如你很少用 AI 操作浏览器，那我还是推荐 Helium 这个，轻量迅速简洁，ego 这个我喜欢的点，就有给 Agent 一个单独的窗口，不会干扰我自己的使用。
5. [**1Password**](https://1password.com/)：今年把我的密码管理逐步迁移到了这个，多平台复用，整体软件品质不错，更多是在 AI 什么都可以破解的年代求一份安全保障，价格也可以接受，用习惯以后，感觉还挺好用的。
6. [**妙言**](https://miaoyan.app/)：一个轻快的原生的 Markdown 笔记应用，默认好用好看，在支持 iPhone 版本后，我几乎每天会打开记录一些东西，每周大伙看到的[潮流周刊](https://weekly.tw93.fun/)就是我用这个 Mac 端来编辑的，包括大伙看到的我的所有文字输出，都是在这个里面草稿来的。
7. [**Grok Bot**](https://x.ai/bot)：可能不是每一个小伙伴喜欢用这个，我感觉他帮了我很多产品经营增长上的忙，包括各种答疑、退款处理、记录问题到 Notion，以及我每天的投资报告、推特日报、潮流日报，均来源于这个帮我在做 Personal Agent。
8. [**UU 远程**](https://uuyc.163.com/)：我感觉这个产品简单易用，在我外出的时候，非常依赖他帮我操作家里的多 Mac 和 Windows 设备，给我帮了很多忙，虽然后面也做付费了，不过我还是非常希望他家可以越做越好。
9. [**Apple Music**](https://www.apple.com.cn/apple-music/)：用过非常多音乐播放器，我还是最喜欢苹果自带的，包月也便宜，歌的质量也高，我听的歌也都在上面，而且我喜欢这个简洁，以及多设备使用，不太喜欢花里胡哨的东西，这个刚刚好。
10. [**Pake**](https://pake.run/)：一个可以很简单把网页打包成桌面 App 的工具，我会把微信读书、李志音乐播放器打包成 Mac 应用，然后用 Raycast 快捷键唤起，很方便，而且可以按照自己喜好定制非常多的东西。
11. [**Shottr**](https://shottr.cc/)：假如要推荐一个最好用最简单的截图工具，还是推荐这个，貌似才 4 刀不买好像也可以用，轻量、我非常喜欢用他来截图窗口、以及滚动截图，用了好几年了。
12. [**微信输入法**](https://z.weixin.qq.com/)：我的所有设备都是用这个输入法，腾讯的赎罪产品，简洁舒服、打字猜的准，特别是最近的语音输入法，我不想装同类的软件，就只用这个，非常好用。

articles.content: 第一时间辞职，然后被董事会请回。 感觉有点像。这次丑闻肯定要有所回应，也不可能什么都不做。 退个屁。暴跌上个一波，暴涨收割一波，哪有那么以退为进。老黄也没能力做这个，决定权不在他那里 前几天被 v2er 教育的，我差点以为美国公司高管人均道德模范。 你觉得黄仁勋，可以随意摆布两党吗？他只是两党的赚钱工具而已！ 真正的世界首富，一周时间震荡几十万亿美元，多空双杀。 丑闻本身现在看更像一个引子，感觉像是美国高层有些人不愿意英伟达持续擦边搞类似 5090d 5090dv2 H200 这种东西卖卡给天朝，所以决定搞黄皮衣，只是没想到黄皮衣主动爆料后辞职影响会这么大，不得已又给请回来了。 经过这一茬，皮衣的主席没拿回来，董事会上面还多了一个国安和进出口管制的权力机构，看起来就是为了制约黄皮衣只想卖卡的心思 不是 1、在他头上多了个董事会主席 2、除 1 之外，还多了很多监管措施，比如类似 “ Nvidia is searching for a brand-new Chief Compliance Officer to oversee compliance across all of Nvidia. Bypassing Huang, the General Counsel, and the Audit Committee. Reporting straight to the Nominating & Corporate Governance Committee.” 3、经过了这些事，也许他会选择在合适的时机联合其他人私有化 Nvidia，比如： “孙正义曾提议借钱帮黄仁勋私有化英伟达 但被婉拒（ https://finance.sina.com.cn/tech/roll/2024-11-16/doc-incwcefn9709124.shtml ）” 或者改变公司治理结构，发行 AB 股，来更稳的掌控这家公司。 当然不是，如果不是美国俊福程序员太多黄仁勋也就被搞掉了，只能说美利坚资源真的太多了，不管是自然资源还是社会资源，可以让这些若只随意挥霍。 仁勋、老黄、勋子
